entry.title: Reflections on Vapor (Building a 3D Smoke Simulator)

link.title: Reflections on Vapor (Building a 3D Smoke Simulator)

entry.content:
Vapor — A Real-Time 3D Smoke Simulator

I joined the Real-Time Graphics Lab at Hankuk University of Foreign Studies as a student researcher, and one of my assignments was to implement three papers on fluid simulation: Stable Fluids, An Unconditionally Stable MacCormack Method, and An Advection-Reflection Solver for Detail-Preserving Fluid Simulation.

That assignment eventually became Vapor, a real-time 3D smoke plume simulator built with C++20 and OpenGL volume ray-marching.

The goal was not simply to reproduce the equations from the papers. I wanted to understand what happens when those ideas have to become an actual working simulator.

What I Learned From the Papers

Each paper contributed something different to the simulator.

Stable Fluids gave me the foundation for understanding how semi-Lagrangian advection can be used to build a stable fluid solver.

I then implemented the MacCormack method to improve the accuracy of semi-Lagrangian advection to second order. Compared to the basic semi-Lagrangian approach, the difference was surprisingly visible: the smoke retained its structure and stayed energetic for much longer.

Finally, I implemented the main idea from the Advection-Reflection method to reduce the kinetic energy loss introduced by the projection step.

The implementation itself was not always as difficult as I expected. The staggered MAC grid initially looked intimidating, but once the data layout and indexing were clear, it became surprisingly intuitive. MacCormack was similar. Seeing the forward and backward advection steps side by side made the algorithm much easier to understand.

The difficult part was everything around those equations.

What Was Not Easy

I started with simple solid walls.

Then I thought an open top boundary would look much better. Instead of having smoke hit an invisible ceiling and bounce back down, I wanted it to naturally leave the simulation domain.

So I tried implementing open boundaries.

The smoke disappeared.

Not gradually. It just blew up and vanished from the screen.

I spent several days trying to figure out what was happening. Eventually, I found that the open boundary implementation introduced inconsistent pressure and velocity boundary conditions, allowing the projection step to produce nonphysical velocity behavior. The problem was not just a visual artifact. The boundary condition was repeatedly destabilizing the simulation, causing the velocity field to grow out of control.

I eventually gave up on the open boundary implementation and went back to solid no-slip walls.

And suddenly, everything worked.

The smoke rose smoothly, curled naturally, and finally looked like smoke.

It was a frustrating experience, but probably one of the most useful parts of the project. I learned that implementing a fluid simulation is not just about translating equations from a paper into code. There are many assumptions and interactions between different parts of the solver that only become apparent when the whole system is actually running.

CPU, GPU, and Debugging

One part I particularly enjoyed was implementing both CPU and GPU versions of the simulation.

The pressure solver and advection step can independently switch between CPU and GPU at runtime. I kept the GLSL compute shaders structurally close to their C++ counterparts, which made it possible to compare the two implementations frame by frame.

This was initially intended mainly for performance comparison, but it became extremely useful for debugging as well.

The GPU implementation could be fast, but when something went wrong, the CPU implementation gave me a much easier reference point. Being able to inspect intermediate values and compare the two paths made debugging much less of a guessing game.

There is something very satisfying about watching that work on the GPU.

What I Took Away From the Project

The biggest lesson was that good debugging data matters enormously.

When a simulation goes wrong, looking at the final rendered smoke is often not enough. The visualization tells you that something is wrong, but not necessarily where or why. Being able to inspect intermediate fields, compare CPU and GPU results, and track how values change over time made a huge difference.

I also learned a lot about working with AI while prototyping software.

AI can make it much faster to get a first implementation running, but the quality of the result depends heavily on how clearly the problem is described and what information is provided. I became much more aware of how to give an AI useful context, how to break a problem into smaller pieces, and how to use it as a prototyping and debugging tool rather than simply asking it to write the whole system.

Most importantly, I learned that reading a paper and implementing a paper are very different things.

A paper can explain the equations and the overall algorithm very clearly. But once you start implementing it, you have to make many additional decisions: how data is laid out, how boundaries are handled, how different stages interact, how to debug numerical instability, and how to verify that an implementation is actually doing what the paper describes.

Those are problems that are easy to overlook when reading the paper alone.

What Comes Next

For now, Vapor still uses a closed simulation domain, so eventually the smoke fills the box.

I may come back to open boundaries someday.

But next time, I know what I’m getting myself into.

For now, I’m just happy watching it work.
entry.summary: What I learned building a real-time 3D fluid simulation with GPU acceleration from scratch.

entry.title: Reflections on Turing Complete (Building a CPU from Scratch)

link.title: Reflections on Turing Complete (Building a CPU from Scratch)

entry.content:
For a long time, CPUs felt almost magical to me. You write code, the processor disappears into a black box, and somehow the correct behavior comes out the other side. I understood the theory from classes, but it still felt abstract.

Building a CPU from scratch in Turing Complete completely changed that.

The biggest surprise was that the arithmetic wasn’t the difficult part. Once I built a Full Adder out of XOR, AND, and OR gates, the ALU stopped feeling mysterious pretty quickly. Addition just became a repeated pattern of simple logic extended across multiple bits. After that, building out more operations felt more like wiring work than “advanced math.”

Control Flow: The Real Challenge

The part that actually took the longest to understand was control flow.

In software, an if statement feels trivial. In hardware, it suddenly becomes a routing problem. Nothing branches magically. You are physically deciding where signals are allowed to go and when they are allowed to move there.

That only really clicked once I started heavily using switches and decoders in my datapath.

Making my own instruction set also helped demystify assembly a lot. I ended up using a simple 4-byte format:

Opcode | Arg1 | Arg2 | Result

What surprised me was how direct instruction decoding felt once I wired it myself. Each byte stopped feeling symbolic and started feeling physical. One part selected registers, another selected an ALU operation, another controlled write-back or jump behavior. An instruction was no longer “a command.” It was just a bundle of control signals.

The Hardest Problem: Conditionals with Immediates

The hardest problem in the entire project ended up being conditional instructions with immediate values.

For normal arithmetic instructions, Arg1 and Arg2 were register addresses, so the datapath stayed consistent. The CPU would read from the registers, feed the values into the ALU, and continue normally.

Conditionals completely broke that assumption.

Suddenly, those same bytes were no longer register selectors. They were actual integer values that needed to go directly into the ALU for comparison and potentially modify the Program Counter.

That meant I had to interrupt my own datapath design with a bunch of switches.

For standard instructions, the CPU would route inputs through the register file like usual. But for conditional instructions, those same paths had to bypass the registers entirely and feed the raw instruction bytes directly into the comparison logic and jump circuitry instead.

That was the moment control flow finally made sense to me.

An if statement at the hardware level is not abstract logic. It is signal routing.

The Why Behind Pipelining

Building a sequential architecture also made performance bottlenecks painfully obvious. When your processor has to fetch, decode, execute, and update state strictly one instruction at a time, you immediately start noticing how much hardware sits idle during each stage. After building even a simple CPU, the reason pipelining exists becomes extremely intuitive.

Conclusion

I still have not implemented proper memory yet, but this project completely changed how I look at computer architecture. Now when I look at datapath diagrams or RISC-V pipeline charts, I do not just see boxes and arrows anymore. I can actually picture the routing decisions underneath them.
entry.summary: How building a virtual CPU changed my perspective on computer architecture, control flow, and hardware design.

entry.title: File Compression Using Huffman Coding
entry.content:
Huffman Encoder / Decoder

Upload file (.txt, .bin): .txt → Encode  |  .bin → Decode

How Huffman Coding Works

Huffman coding is a popular lossless data compression algorithm. The core idea is to assign variable-length codes to input characters, with lengths based on the frequencies of the corresponding characters. The most frequent characters get the shortest codes and the least frequent characters get the longest codes.

Because the codes are generated using a binary tree (the Huffman tree), they are prefix codes, which means the bit representation of any character is never a prefix of the bit representation of any other character. This is crucial because it allows the encoded bitstream to be decoded unambiguously without needing any special delimiters between characters.

My handwritten notes on Huffman Coding.

Implementation Details

My implementation breaks the process down into several specific, manageable steps:

  1. Count Frequencies: The getFrequencies function scans the input text and builds a frequency map of each character.
  2. Build the Huffman Tree: buildTree takes the frequencies and constructs a priority queue (using a sorted array for simplicity). It repeatedly takes the two nodes with the lowest frequencies and merges them into a parent node until only the root node remains.
  3. Generate Code Table: The tree is traversed recursively by buildCodeTable to generate a binary string (‘0’ for left, ‘1’ for right) for each leaf node.
  4. Encoding: encode converts the original text into a single, long string of '0's and '1's using the code table.
  5. Binary Packing: Since JavaScript natively stores strings using UTF-16, a string of "0101" uses way more memory than actual bits. packTo32BitChunks converts this pseudo-bitstream into a Uint32Array by packing 32 bits into each integer.
  6. Binary Serialization: To save it as an actual file, serializeToBinary creates a byte buffer using standard DataView and Uint8Array. It writes a header (so the decoder knows the code table), padding information (so we know how many trailing bits to ignore in the last chunk), and the compressed data itself.
  7. Decoding: Decoding reverses the process. We parse the file bytes, read the header to reconstruct the code table, unpack the Uint32Array back into our stream of bits, and traverse our reverse code mapping to get the original text back.

Future Improvements

While this implementation is fully functional and compresses text efficiently, there are some areas for improvement in the future:

  • Eliminate Intermediate String Allocation: Currently, the code builds a giant string of "1"s and "0"s during encoding before packing it into 32-bit integers. This can cause high memory usage for large files. Writing directly to a bit buffer during encoding would be much more memory-efficient.
  • Tree Storage Format: Right now, the header directly stores a simple text serialization of the code table (e.g., a:01\nb:10). It would be more compact to serialize the structure of the Huffman tree itself, or just the frequencies, saving header overhead.
  • Adaptive Huffman Coding: This current implementation is robust, but it requires two passes over the data (one to get frequencies, one to encode). Adaptive (or dynamic) Huffman coding updates the tree dynamically as symbols are read, requiring only a single pass.
  • Handling Binary Files: Right now the input is strictly treated as text characters. Updating the initial frequency map to use raw bytes (0-255) instead of string characters would allow testing compression on not just text, but arbitrary file types (like images or executables).
